subject: chemistry

items.q: In diamond, how many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form, and with what?
items.correct: Four covalent bonds, with four other carbon atoms
items.misconception: Four covalent bonds, within a small carbon molecule
items.why: Simple molecular substances are taught alongside diamond and both are covalent. Students carry across the rule that covalent substances melt easily because the forces between the molecules are weak. Check first whether the substance is made of separate molecules. Diamond has none; the covalent bonds run through the whole crystal, so they are the bonds that must be broken, and that is why the melting point is very high.
items.random_wrong: Four covalent bonds, with atoms of other elements

items.q: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
items.correct: All four outer electrons of each carbon atom are held in bonds
items.misconception: The carbon atoms in diamond do not contain any electrons
items.why: Students shorten 'no free electrons' to 'no electrons' when they revise, and they are rarely asked to say what the electrons in diamond are doing instead. Always say what the electrons are doing. In diamond all four outer electrons are held in bonds; in graphite one per atom is delocalised, and that single difference is why graphite conducts and diamond does not.
items.random_wrong: Its molecules are packed too tightly for electrons to move

items.q: Diamond has a very high melting point. What is the reason?
items.correct: A very large number of strong covalent bonds must be broken
items.misconception: The weak forces between the diamond molecules must be overcome
items.why: Simple molecular substances are taught alongside diamond and both are covalent. Students carry across the rule that covalent substances melt easily because the forces between the molecules are weak. Check first whether the substance is made of separate molecules. Diamond has none; the covalent bonds run through the whole crystal, so they are the bonds that must be broken, and that is why the melting point is very high.
items.random_wrong: Diamond has no free electrons to carry energy through it

items.q: Which feature of diamond's structure explains why it is very hard?
items.correct: Every atom is held in place by four strong covalent bonds
items.misconception: The layers of carbon atoms are unable to slide past each other
items.why: Students link soft to weak. Because graphite rubs off onto paper they assume whatever holds it together must be feeble, and they never separate the bonding inside a layer from the forces between layers. Ask where the sliding happens. Graphite gives way between the layers, where there are no covalent bonds at all. Inside each layer the covalent bonds are strong, which is why graphite still has a very high melting point.
items.random_wrong: There are no delocalised electrons anywhere in the structure

items.q: In graphite, each carbon atom forms:
items.correct: three covalent bonds, forming layers of hexagonal rings
items.misconception: three covalent bonds, plus weak covalent bonds between layers
items.why: Students expect anything that holds a solid together to be bonds of some kind, and a 'weak covalent bond' feels like a sensible compromise between the layers being joined and the layers sliding. The specification is precise: layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers. Every covalent bond in graphite lies inside a layer.
items.random_wrong: four covalent bonds, as in every other form of carbon

items.q: What lies between the layers of hexagonal rings in graphite?
items.correct: No covalent bonds at all, only weak forces of attraction
items.misconception: Weak covalent bonds, which are broken easily by rubbing
items.why: Students expect anything that holds a solid together to be bonds of some kind, and a 'weak covalent bond' feels like a sensible compromise between the layers being joined and the layers sliding. The specification is precise: layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers. Every covalent bond in graphite lies inside a layer.
items.random_wrong: The fourth outer electron of each atom, fixed in position

items.q: In graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is:
items.correct: delocalised, and free to move through the structure
items.misconception: left on its own atom, in the outer shell where it began
items.why: Bonding is first taught with electrons drawn in fixed shells, so a spare electron is pictured sitting where it started, and delocalised is read as merely meaning 'not used in a bond'. Delocalised means the electron is no longer attached to any one atom. That is precisely why graphite conducts electricity and why graphite is described as being similar to a metal.
items.random_wrong: used to bond weakly to the layer above and below

items.q: Graphite is soft enough to leave a mark on paper. Why?
items.correct: Its layers can slide because no covalent bonds join them
items.misconception: The covalent bonds within graphite are weak and break easily
items.why: Students link soft to weak. Because graphite rubs off onto paper they assume whatever holds it together must be feeble, and they never separate the bonding inside a layer from the forces between layers. Ask where the sliding happens. Graphite gives way between the layers, where there are no covalent bonds at all. Inside each layer the covalent bonds are strong, which is why graphite still has a very high melting point.
items.random_wrong: Its delocalised electrons let the atoms slip past each other

items.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
items.correct: One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and moves
items.misconception: Its layers slide over each other and carry the charge
items.why: Both softness and conduction are explained from the layer structure, so students fuse the two explanations and use the movement of layers to account for the movement of charge. Keep the two properties apart. Softness comes from there being no covalent bonds between the layers; conduction comes from the one delocalised electron contributed by each carbon atom.
items.random_wrong: Each carbon atom holds a spare electron in its outer shell

items.q: Graphite is soft, yet its melting point is very high. Why?
items.correct: The covalent bonds within each layer are strong and numerous
items.misconception: Its melting point is in fact low, which is why it is soft
items.why: Hardness and melting point are both treated as 'how tough is it', so a soft solid is assumed to be easy to melt as well. Hardness and melting point measure different things. Graphite gives way between its layers, which makes it soft, but melting it means breaking the strong covalent bonds inside the layers.
items.random_wrong: The weak forces between layers must be broken to melt it

items.q: In what way is graphite similar to a metal?
items.correct: Graphite has delocalised electrons, as metals do
items.misconception: Graphite is a metal, so it behaves in the same way
items.why: Conducting electricity is the test students use to identify a metal, and delocalised electrons are first met in metallic bonding, so both clues point them the wrong way. The specification states a similarity, not an identity: graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons. Its atoms are still held by covalent bonds, and carbon is a non-metal.
items.random_wrong: Graphite is held together by metallic bonds as well

items.q: Graphene is best described as:
items.correct: a single layer of graphite, one atom thick
items.misconception: a hollow ball of carbon atoms, like a fullerene
items.why: All three are met in the same lesson as new forms of carbon built from hexagonal rings, so students file them under a single heading and stop distinguishing them. Sort them by shape. Graphene is a flat sheet one atom thick with nothing above or below it. A fullerene is a closed hollow shape, which is why a nanotube counts as a fullerene but a graphene sheet does not.
items.random_wrong: a stack of graphite layers, very thinly sliced

items.q: Why is graphene useful in electronics and in composites?
items.correct: It has delocalised electrons and strong covalent bonds
items.misconception: It is one atom thick, so it bends and stretches very easily
items.why: Thin things in everyday life tear, and students judge the sheet by how thick it is rather than by the bonds holding its atoms together. Judge strength from the bonding. The sheet is thin, but every bond in it is a strong covalent bond, so adding graphene to a composite strengthens it without adding much mass.
items.random_wrong: It is hollow, so other substances can be held inside it

items.q: Which statement about fullerenes is correct?
items.correct: They are hollow molecules based on hexagonal rings of carbon
items.misconception: They are built from hexagonal rings of carbon and nothing else
items.why: Hexagonal rings dominate every diagram of graphite and graphene, so students carry the rule over and do not notice the other ring sizes in a fullerene. Look for the odd rings in a fullerene diagram. Rings of five or seven carbon atoms sit among the hexagons, and they are what let a flat arrangement of rings close up into a hollow shape.
items.random_wrong: They are all spheres containing exactly 60 carbon atoms

items.q: Which of these describes Buckminsterfullerene?
items.correct: The first fullerene discovered, C60, with a spherical shape
items.misconception: A cylinder with a very high length to diameter ratio
items.why: The word fullerene is introduced with a picture of a sphere, so students treat the round shape rather than the hollow carbon cage as the defining feature, and then need a separate box for tubes. Fullerene covers any molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape. A nanotube is a fullerene that has been drawn out into a cylinder rather than closed into a ball.
items.random_wrong: A sphere of 60 atoms, and the only shape a fullerene takes

items.q: Which statement about carbon nanotubes is correct?
items.correct: They are cylindrical fullerenes, very long and very thin
items.misconception: They are not fullerenes, because fullerenes are spherical
items.why: The word fullerene is introduced with a picture of a sphere, so students treat the round shape rather than the hollow carbon cage as the defining feature, and then need a separate box for tubes. Fullerene covers any molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape. A nanotube is a fullerene that has been drawn out into a cylinder rather than closed into a ball.
items.random_wrong: Their high length to diameter ratio makes them wide tubes

items.q: A diagram shows a flat sheet of hexagonal carbon rings, one atom thick, with no layers above or below it. What does the diagram show?
items.correct: Graphene, a single layer of graphite one atom thick
items.misconception: A fullerene, because fullerenes are sheets of hexagons
items.why: All three are met in the same lesson as new forms of carbon built from hexagonal rings, so students file them under a single heading and stop distinguishing them. Sort them by shape. Graphene is a flat sheet one atom thick with nothing above or below it. A fullerene is a closed hollow shape, which is why a nanotube counts as a fullerene but a graphene sheet does not.
items.random_wrong: Graphite, because graphite is made of hexagonal rings

items.q: Which of these is an example of a use of fullerenes?
items.correct: Delivering drugs into the body inside their hollow cages
items.misconception: Making thick cables that can be seen with the naked eye
items.why: Students read the word length and think about absolute size, forgetting that a ratio compares two measurements of the same object against each other. A ratio compares. Length divided by diameter is very large because the diameter is tiny, and it is that extreme thinness that makes nanotubes useful in nanotechnology.
items.random_wrong: Acting as a single flat sheet inside touchscreen glass

items.q: Carbon nanotubes are added to the frame of a tennis racket. Why?
items.correct: They are very strong, so they reinforce the material used
items.misconception: They are thin, so they let the frame bend much more easily
items.why: Thin things in everyday life tear, and students judge the sheet by how thick it is rather than by the bonds holding its atoms together. Judge strength from the bonding. The sheet is thin, but every bond in it is a strong covalent bond, so adding graphene to a composite strengthens it without adding much mass.
items.random_wrong: They are wide tubes, so they fill the space inside the frame

items.q: Do all fullerenes have the same shape and size as C60?
items.correct: No. Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes of many kinds. Buckminsterfullerene, C60, was simply the first one to be discovered and it is the one with a spherical shape.
items.misconception: Every fullerene is a sphere made of exactly 60 carbon atoms.
items.why: C60 is usually the only fullerene students see drawn, and the football picture is so memorable that it becomes their definition of the whole family. What defines a fullerene is a hollow shape built mainly from hexagonal rings, not a particular number of atoms. Carbon nanotubes are fullerenes too, and they are cylinders.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are diamond and graphite made from?
items.correct: Both are made from carbon atoms and nothing else. They differ in how those atoms are bonded: four covalent bonds from each carbon atom in diamond, three in graphite.
items.misconception: Diamond and graphite behave so differently that they must contain different elements, or graphite must have something extra mixed into it.
items.why: The two substances look and behave nothing alike, so students assume the difference must come from different ingredients rather than from a different arrangement of the same atoms. Compare the bonding, not the ingredients. Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds in diamond and three in graphite, and that difference alone accounts for every property in the specification.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.2.3 Structure and bonding of carbon
